title: East Antrim: Larne to Kilwaughter
standfirst: The Kilwaughter James of 1669 is probably the later overseer and elder, alongside John’s already-probable continuity. The Larne, Glenarm and later Kilwaughter families retain their uncertain exact relationships.
question: Can the early Larne, Glenarm and Kilwaughter occurrences be connected by a record-defined household?
answer: James’s 1669-to-later-elder identity is now probable on the combined John–James local sequence; that strengthens the account without proving their parents or the later joining generations. Not yet. Robert at Larne in 1653, Elizabeth at Glenarm and James and John at Kilwaughter in 1669 are documented local occurrences. The later 1764 lease proves Robert Glasgow’s son James, but it does not identify Robert’s father or connect that family to the seventeenth-century people.

chapters.title: Kilwaughter: James’s 1669–1726 continuity is probable
body: The preferred identification is one James Glasgow from the Kilwaughter Demesne hearth household of 1669 to the Kilwaughter overseer of probably 29 May 1701 and the later elder marked deceased in 1726. Assess that continuity as probable rather than unresolved. The hearth roll places Jo and James Glascho consecutively in the same demesne, records 5347–5348. The later congregational extracts again contain both names acting for Kilwaughter: John senior in 1700 and an unmarked John in 1700/01, whose individual identity remains open, and James as overseer in probably 1701. John’s already-probable continuity supplies a coherent parallel ageing household, rather than leaving James’s later occurrence as an isolated name match. James’s later elder, 1722 commissioner and 1727 Kilwater probate-index accounts were already assessed as probably one man. The repeated local pairing, the particular district served and an ordinary adult generation in 1700/01 together favour continuity over an otherwise unattested replacement James. The preference uses the combined local sequence; no literal same-man clause is required.

The inference is not documented identity. The later men never occur together in the same reviewed minute, the 1669 roll does not state a kin relationship, and similar spellings are not independent identifiers. Kilwaughter Demesne and the later Kilwaughter district are compatible but not identical address statements. A father-and-son succession or another local James remains possible. Assuming an adult aged at least 21 in 1669 would make James at least about 74 in 1722 and 78 in 1726; those are conditional age calculations, not recorded ages or a new birth bound. His local commission in 1722 is compatible with advanced age, but the long career is the strongest reason for caution. No age at death, occupation, holding or named relative equates the occurrences. The missing 1701–1721 session sequence leaves a real gap. Porter’s 1699–1701 extracts are a printed transcription of a manuscript copy; the later extracts and lost probate index do not independently prove the earlier identity. The probable grade is an overall inference across the groups, not the product of independent probabilities. Neither the 1726 death annotation nor the 1727 probate is newly assigned to a separate earlier James; they remain events of the later elder whose identification with the 1669 man is now probable.

This strengthens the identity at the head of James’s existing 104-profile pre-1850 working branch. The number describes retained profile accounts, including uncertain descendants and unresolved identities. John’s 1669-to-1700 identity was already probable and is not counted as a new upgrade. Exact kinship between John and James remains possible: brother, father and son, uncle and nephew or cousin are not distinguished. Glasgow-3970 of Larne remains their uncertain proposed father. The Scottish Robert and James comparisons, the later South Side family represented by Glasgow-1502 and all mothers retain their separate assessments. No father or mother is regraded, no profile is merged, and no birth, death or place field is changed. Working, supported and confidently marked paternal connectivity are unchanged. This is a re-evaluation of the maintained source readings, not a newly found record or fresh original inspection. Nothing is saved to live WikiTree.

chapters.title: A provisional Scottish parentage and the Belfast shipmaster
body: Select Robert Glasgow-1027 and Jonet Cunningham-20923 as the uncertain working father and mother of Robert Glaskow of Larne, Glasgow-3970, through the existing possible identity with their son Robert Glasgow-1078, baptised at Glasgow on 17 November 1618. The 1653 Larne account gives no age or parents, and its before-1625 birth boundary permits the 1618 child; that child would have been about 23 during the alleged 1641 events and 35 in 1653. The Scottish child has no established later fate that excludes this adult account. Choose the already recorded possible identity as the working family explanation, at low confidence. The baptism names both parents, so the maternal selection is assessed from that same explicit child clause, not from a Cunningham surname association in Ulster. Both adult parent links depend on the uncertain identity and remain uncertain; the baptism’s direct parentage must not be transferred as proof of the Larne man’s origins.

Select Robert of Larne-3970 as Captain James Glasgow-3172’s uncertain working father. This adopts the existing possible son-or-younger-relative comparison: Larne, Belfast and Kilwaughter form the north-east Antrim setting of the recorded Robert and later James, and an older Robert active in 1641–1653 can precede a shipmaster active by 1667. James commanded the Blessing of Saltcoats in the 1667 Macartney correspondence and the James of Belfast in 1679. These are compatible Scottish-west-coast/Antrim associations, not a parent clause. Son is selected over the unresolved younger-relative alternatives for one provisional paternal route; no mother is selected for James.

Robert-1078 and Robert-3970 remain separate profile accounts of a possible single man; the selected parents do not establish two distinct Robert sons or an identity merge. No record joins the 1618 baptism to Larne, supplies the Larne man’s Scottish origin, or rules out another Robert. The 1666 John of Portrush shipmaster is a further possible identity, not an occupation proved for either Robert; the later Robert/Rachel household remains separate. James-3172, the Scottish child James-3971 of 1645, and the Kilwaughter James-1081 may be one, two or three men. All accounts remain; no identity among those James groups is selected. A child baptised in 1645 could have been a shipmaster aged about 22 in 1667, assuming infant baptism, but that is compatibility only. The father named in that 1645 record is not independently identified with the 1618 child. John-3913’s circa-1630 and Captain James’s circa-1640 births are inherited estimates, not dates that establish or exclude a generation. If John’s 1630 were literal and the Larne man were born in 1618, fatherhood at about twelve would be an important chronological objection; both the age estimate and John’s uncertain paternal attachment require testing. No birth year is changed to force the selected route. Captain James could instead be a nephew, other relative, unrelated namesake, or a member of the Saltcoats sailor John-4152’s family; the named Saltcoats vessel makes that a real competing route, not evidence that John was his father. The two women Cunningham-20923 and Cunningham-22604 are distinct: the elder is the named 1618 mother, the younger the named mother in the 1645 James record. Neither that younger maternity nor a marriage to her is transferred to the Larne adult or captain through these selections. The existing uncertain Kilwaughter father links remain uncertain; none becomes proved by joining their supposed ancestor to Scotland. The Larne allegations are hearsay, not a judicial finding of guilt, and the 1686 will reference is not a proved death date. No new original inspection, certainty upgrade, live WikiTree edit or identity merge is claimed. Connectivity counts profile accounts and does not resolve the possible duplicates.

chapters.title: A Larne occurrence
body: A deposition records Robert Glaskow at Larne. The testimony does not give an age, wife, child or Scottish origin.
The Scottish Robert baptised in 1618 is a possible comparison only and remains separate.

chapters.title: Three names in the hearth-money roll
body: The County Antrim roll records Elizabeth at Glenarm Town and James and John at Kilwaughter Demesne. James and John appear beside one another, but the roll states no kinship.
Later congregational appearances make continuity for John and association with James plausible, not a stated relationship.

chapters.title: Later records require separate tests
body: Congregational extracts place a John senior and James in Kilwaughter business, while later Larne and Kilwaughter households have their own evidence. Same place and repeated names do not supply parentage.
The documented reconstruction of Robert and James belongs to the separate Larne & Kilwaughter family study.

chapters.title: One later father–son statement
body: The Ballykeel lease explicitly calls James Glasgow the son of Robert Glasgow. It is direct evidence for that pair.
It does not bridge from either man to the 1653 or 1669 householders, and this study does not extend the pedigree beyond that boundary.

clusters.title: Larne, Glenarm and Kilwaughter occurrences
clusters.summary: A deposition, hearth-money roll and later congregational extracts establish named people in the locality.
clusters.boundary: No source names a founding couple or tells how the seventeenth-century people were related.

clusters.title: Later Larne and Kilwaughter households
clusters.summary: Several later households are record-supported, including the Robert–James lease relationship.
clusters.boundary: Their links to the early occurrences remain unproved; see the dedicated family reconstruction.
